doc.title: Dan Wall and Adam Nussbaum interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 19, 2001

title: Working with singers and supporting great players
summary: Wall recalls Dakota Staton, Maxine Sullivan and Sheila Jordan; both talk about accompanying singers and finding common ground.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them

blocks.x: You’ve had the opportunity to work with vocalists much and is it different?
Yeah I used to do a lot of work in the 80s with Dakota Staton.

Yeah, “The Late Late Show.” And I had always loved her records and that was a lot of fun for me to be out doing gigs with her. She didn’t drive so a lot of times I would pick her up for the gig or take her back after the gig or something. But musically that was great, and there was another singer, Maxine Sullivan, who I did a record actually also with Maxine that got a lot of nice attention. And that was a lot of fun. Sheila Jordan. My wife is a singer, is a really good singer. We’ve enjoyed being able to work together all of these years and to write together or do projects. But that’s another, you know that’s a funny subject too because a lot of musicians are so caught up in looking in one direction

that vocalists, they block this whole concept out. “No I don’t want to work with a vocalist,” like it’s a waste of time. But with the right person it’s another zone. You can create incredible things but—

You have to be very sensitive to the situation. I mean you have to respect what the song is. I mean they’re trying to sing a lyric. You have to make sure you can always hear that lyric. You have to give them the right kind of support so they can get it out there. And it requires a certain sensitivity. I mean working with Stan Getz was like working with a great singer, because I mean really, the way he could sing out a melody, I mean he was somebody where he didn’t even have to improvise on a song. He could just play a ballad and play the melody. You didn’t even need to hear him blow on it. He brought a complete life and beautiful expression to just a melody. And you know when you work with a singer you have to be respectful for what they need. You need to support them, but you can’t get in their way. I enjoy it. If it’s a good singer, I love it.
But then see that’s always the thing.
Because yeah well okay what about a horn player? What do you enjoy playing with a bad horn player? That’s what I always try to tell people to wake them up, like listen to what you’re singing.

It’s like when I listen to somebody, somebody goes well you seem to play with a lot of guitar players. Or you seem to play with a lot of this. I say well it’s not the instrument that I dig playing with, it’s the person who’s playing it. Like I’m more concerned with what the person is saying than what the instrument is. I mean what’s the person, what’s the personality, what’s the voice? I mean any great artist on any instrument, any great artist, even visual has a vibe, has a voice. And that’s what I listen for. You know what are you saying, what’s the story? Not like is it a guitar is it a piano, it’s like what are you saying? I mean some singers are great. Some aren’t. Some horn players are great. Some aren’t. That’s a good thing you said that.

I think it’s a good point too from the accompanist standpoint that they have to not only bring good music but a good personality to make things cohesive. Get that Kum-ba-ya you were talking about. Right?

I know when I worked with somebody like Al Cohn or Buddy DeFranco or Charlie Rouse, you know you find a way, they play a certain way. They play great. They played great, well Buddy is still living, all in their own ways, but you find a way of interacting with that and if you enjoy the way that you are interacting with it then you have fun working with this person. It doesn’t matter if he’s playing clarinet. You find Kum-ba-ya.
